newsitem.title: USA: Dole, saying 'it hurts,' concedes defeat.
newsitem.headline: Dole, saying 'it hurts,' concedes defeat.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole on Tuesday formally conceded defeat to President Bill Clinton, but still called himself "the most optimistic man in America."

"It hurts to lose an election, but stay involved and keep fighting the good fight," Dole told cheering supporters at a hotel in Washington. Echoing a statement he made throughout his campaign, he added, "I'm still the most optimistic man in America."
Dole, with his wife Elizabeth and daughter Robin at his side, struggled to keep his emotions in check after an arduous campaign. Some of his supporters openly cried.
"I have never been prouder in my life than to have been the Republican nominee for the president of the United States," he told the crowd.
"I talked to President Clinton and I congratulated him."
Gracious in defeat, he stilled those in the audience who booed at the name of Clinton. "I've said repeatedly in this campaign the president was my opponent, not my enemy and I wish him well..."

He drew a laugh when he said: "I was just thinking on the way down the stairs that tomorrow will be the first day in my life when I don't have anything to do." Dole had spent 35 years in Congress when he resigned as Senate majority leader in May to concentrate on his run for president.

He offered consolation to his campaign aides and supporters when he declared that although the Republicans had lost the presidential race, "We're gonna keep the Senate, We're gonna keep the House (of Representatives)."
Television networks predicted his party would retain control of both houses of Congress.

Dole did not address what he would do next. His career had been in public service, starting in 1951 with local offices in his hometown of Russell, Kansas, after recuperating from Second World War combat wounds that nearly killed him and left him with a useless right arm.
"I'm going to sit back for a few days and then I'm gonna start standing up for what I think is right for America," Dole said.
He told television personality David Frost recently that if he did lose he would like to work with other disabled people.
Dole graciously thanked his staff and urged young people to carry on the fight.
"I leave with a full heart and a fervent prayer that we will meet again and we will meet often," he said.
Earlier Tuesday, before polls had closed in many Western states, including California, a Dole spokesman issued a statement conceding the election and later retracted it.
"The fact is Bob Dole has conceded nothing," spokesman Nelson Warfield said in a statement, adding that an earlier concession of defeat had been "prematurely released to some news outlets."
The earlier statement, which also bore Warfield's name, clearly said Dole had lost the White House race.
"Bob Dole has completed his last political mission with courage and honour," the earlier statement read.

"Even in defeat, he has much to claim in the way of success. Bob Dole led his party in this election representing trust and conservative principles. With Republicans headed toward retaining the leadership of Congress, this country on the broadest front endorsed what Bob Dole stood for."
